To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the standard classical expression for dynamic Stokes shift in solution is modified by a quantum correction which is negligible when the pump pulse is tuned close to the maximum of the absorption spectrum, and which is significant when the pump pulse frequency is tuned to a far sideband.

1) a simple formula for the DSS is obtained that generalizes the standard classical expression and that includes the effect of finite duration pump pulse; 2) the quantum correction to this generalized expression is negligible for the pump pulse close to the maximum of the absorption band; 3) for the pump pulse far from the maximum of the band, a deviation from the classical formula is expected.

the standard formula for DSS, which is based on the assumption that the pump pulse is infinitely short, is modified by the finite duration of the pump pulse, but that the modification is not significant when the pump pulse frequency is close to the absorption maximum of the chromophor.

the DSS is a very useful tool for the investigation of the dynamics of the solute-solvent interaction in solution.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the dynamic Stokes shift is a very useful tool to characterize solvation dynamics, but the interpretation of the DSS in terms of the average energy difference of the chromophores in the excited and ground states requires a careful analysis of the experimental conditions.
a pump pulse of a finite duration is required for a quantitative determination of the dynamic Stokes shift.

the standard formula for the normalized dynamic Stokes shift, which has been used for decades, is valid only if the pump pulse is very short compared to the relaxation times in the system, and if the pump pulse frequency is close to the peak in the absorption spectrum.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the standard formula for DSS can be used to analyze the time-evolution of DSS when the frequency of excitation is close to the absorption maximum, but the DSS expression can be corrected to include the effect of the finite duration of the pump pulse.
the DSS formula for an ultrafast pump of finite duration is a simple function of the pump pulse frequency and the dielectric relaxation time of the solvent.

the dynamic Stokes shift is a useful tool for the characterization of the relaxation of the solute, but the standard classical formula should not be used without considering its limits of applicability.
